query: Consider the following context: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered promising candidate materials for next‐generation nuclear reactors due to their superior mechanical strength, irradiation resistance, and thermal stability at high temperatures. However, the significant positive heat of mixing between refractory alloying elements and Cu, commonly used in cooling systems, poses challenges in forming composite structures. In that context, which method can be used for large‐scale reaction and stable microstructure, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Implementing a machine-learning-driven parameter screening and optimization of mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering conditions will enable the formation of stable refractory high-entropy alloy–copper (RHEA–Cu) composites at scale, despite their large positive enthalpy of mixing.
generation.material_initial_state: Powder mixture of refractory high-entropy alloy elements and copper.
generation.intervention: A data-driven (machine-learning) approach to tune mechanical alloying parameters (milling time, ball-to-powder ratio, etc.) and spark plasma sintering conditions (temperature, pressure, dwell times).
generation.conditions: Mechanical alloying in an inert environment, followed by spark plasma sintering at optimized dwell time, temperature, and pressure, as identified by ML-based parameter screening.
generation.structural_mediator: Dense, uniformly distributed RHEA–Cu phases with minimal undesired phase segregation.
generation.mechanism: Rapid, controlled solid-state reactions and consolidation reduce unchecked diffusion and thermodynamic driving forces for phase separation, guided by ML-assisted fine-tuning of process variables.
generation.predicted_outcome: Consistently high-density, stable microstructure RHEA–Cu composites, retaining mechanical integrity and thermal stability at high temperatures.
generation.baseline: Conventional trial-and-error powder metallurgy methods struggle with controlling phase separation due to high positive heat of mixing with copper, especially at scale.
generation.boundary: Applicability primarily for moderate Cu content and for carefully formulated RHEA compositions; success depends on robust ML models and consistent powder quality.
generation.uncertainty: Full industrial-scale trials remain untested; the reliability of data-driven insights depends on the quality and breadth of the underlying parameter datasets.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of powder blends of RHEA–Cu with varying composition ratios and systematically vary mechanical alloying and SPS parameters according to a machine-learning design of experiments.
measurements: Phase constitution and grain size via X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy
Phase stability and chemical homogeneity via EDS or EBSD mapping
Density measurements after consolidation (e.g., Archimedes method)
Thermal stability tests (e.g., annealing at various times/temperatures)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If any parameter set fails to produce a homogeneous, stable RHEA–Cu microstructure above a target density and mechanical performance threshold, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. However, most of these RHEAs are generally characterized with high density and poor high temperature oxidation

This paper reports the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of a low-density Al 0.3 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) prepared by means of a combination of mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS). Prior to sintering, the morphology, chemical homogeneity and crystal structures of the powders were thoroughly investigated by varying the milling times to find optimal conditions for densification. The sintered bulk RHEAs were produced with diverse feedstock powder conditions. The microstructural development of the materials was analyzed in terms of phase composition and constitution, chemical homogeneity, and crystallographic properties. Hardness and elastic constants also were measured. The calculation of phase diagrams (CALPHAD) was performed to predict the phase changes in the alloy, and the results were compared with the experiments. Milling time seems to play a significant role in the contamination level of the sintered materials. Even though a protective atmosphere was used in the entire manufacturing process, carbide formation was detected in the sintered bulks as early as after 3 h of powder milling. decision.trend: Mechanical-alloying-based powder routes combined with rapid consolidation (e.g., spark plasma sintering) have repeatedly proven effective for synthesizing refractory high-entropy alloys with stable microstructures at high temperatures. In 2018, two approaches were demonstrated: (a) mechanical alloying of RHEA powders for 40 h followed by spark plasma sintering, enabling fine-grained, high-strength microstructures (PMC5978046); and (b) high-energy ball milling with in-situ ceramic reinforcement introduced during spark plasma sintering for added high-temperature strength (PMC7513042). These works establish that powder-based processing can produce stable, high-performance RHEAs on a reasonably large scale. However, none have yet tackled the specific challenge of incorporating Cu into RHEAs when the large positive enthalpy of mixing might drive detrimental phase separation, leaving the development of integrative process parameters an open challenge.
decision.unsolved: Despite the demonstrated success of powder metallurgy methods in fabricating high-strength, thermally stable refractory high-entropy alloys, the issue of forming stable RHEA–Cu composites remains unresolved. The strong tendency for phase separation, driven by the large positive heat of mixing between refractory elements and Cu, has not yet been addressed by systematic parameter optimization that would enable scaled-up manufacturing while preserving microstructural stability.
decision.lever: Implementing a machine-learning-driven parameter screening and optimization for mechanical alloying and sintering variables (e.g., milling duration, ball-to-powder ratio, sintering temperature, dwell time) to accelerate the discovery of conditions that prevent phase separation and ensure stable RHEA–Cu composites during large-scale fabrication.
decision.why: Prior studies prove powder-based approaches (mechanical alloying + SPS) can achieve uniform RHEA microstructures on practical scales, but further progress requires systematically navigating the complex space of process conditions to counteract the large positive enthalpy of mixing with Cu. A data-driven approach can efficiently explore and refine process parameters, guiding the manufacturing of stable, scalable RHEA–Cu composites for nuclear applications.
